Imagine you’re on a data project and need to bring a group of analysts up to speed quickly.

You look at the usual vendor courses and see a long list of fees,
 prerequisites,
 and limited seats.

Now picture a free, globally accessible training program from Snowflake that anyone can join,
 no cost,
 no gatekeeping.

The contrast is stark – learning that used to be a hurdle becomes a simple click away.

Snowflake’s initiative opens a catalog of data and AI lessons,
 covering fundamentals and hands‑on labs.

For data engineers, that means you can recommend a vetted learning path without worrying about budget approval.

For analysts, it provides a clear roadmap from basics to advanced topics,
 all in one place.

The practical upside is you can schedule a team learning day,
 assign the free modules,
 and see progress in real time.

You also get a community of learners worldwide,
 so questions get answered quickly.

My takeaway is to treat this resource as a first stop when upskilling,
 before looking at paid options.

Give it a try and see how quickly your team can move from theory to practice.

news_posts.post_content:
Choosing an LLM based solely on headline numbers can lead to costly mismatches.
A recent benchmark showed Gemini 4 Carbon scoring 60 while Claude Opus 5.5 posted 2026 on the same test – shattered.io.
The key lesson is to treat any single metric as a data point, not a verdict.
Evaluation should be anchored in three pillars:
 relevance to your task,
 consistency across inputs,
 and cost per token.
Relevance means the model produces answers that fit the domain language and accuracy you need.
Consistency checks whether performance holds when you vary prompts, formats, or data slices.
Cost per token captures the economic impact of scaling the model in production.
A quick checklist you can run after any benchmark report:
 • Verify the test set matches your real‑world data.
 • Run at least three prompt variations per query.
 • Calculate average cost for the same throughput.
 • Compare results against a baseline you already use.
Fact: Gemini 4 Carbon achieved a score of 60 on the shared benchmark.
Interpretation: The higher score suggests better performance on that specific metric, but it does not guarantee superiority on your use case.
By applying the checklist, you turn a headline into an actionable decision.
My recommendation is to embed this three‑pillar check into every model‑selection process, rather than relying on a single headline figure.
